messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was thirty-four when it happened, a year into his postdoctoral fellowship at a community mental health clinic in Chicago. A colleague he had trusted—another psychologist, a man he had supervised interns with, shared lunches with—invited him to his apartment after a conference. Kwame remembered the door clicking shut behind him, the sound of the deadbolt sliding into place, and the sudden, sickening shift in the other man’s tone. He remembered thinking, *I can talk my way out of this*, and then realizing, as the other man’s hand clamped over his mouth, that he could not. The assault lasted perhaps twenty minutes, but Kwame’s memory of it was not a story with a beginning, middle, and end; it was a series of snapshots: the pressure of a forearm against his throat, the ceiling light fixture that was missing one bulb, the smell of the other man’s cologne, the click of the deadbolt again when it was over and he was told to leave.

He did not go to the police. He did not tell his supervisor. He showered, he went to work the next day, and he told himself he was fine. But within a week, he could not sit in his office without keeping the door slightly ajar. When a male client arrived for a session, Kwame found himself scanning the room for exits, his back to the wall, the client’s chair positioned so that the door was always in Kwame’s line of sight. He began to dread afternoons when he had back-to-back sessions, because he could not relax between them. He would stand in the hallway instead of sitting in his office. He stopped using the staff break room because it had no windows and only one door. He told himself it was just an adjustment period, a phase.

Months passed. Kwame’s sleep became a battlefield. He would lie in bed, his body rigid, listening to the sounds of his apartment building—the creak of floorboards, the hum of the furnace—and he would be unable to let his guard down. He felt as though some part of him was always on watch, even in the safest places. He started checking the locks on his bedroom door three, four times a night. He eventually moved his mattress into the living room, where he could sleep with his back against the wall and a clear view of the front door. It helped, a little.

At work, a male colleague once made a passing comment about the coverage of a high-profile sexual assault case in the news. *Another one*, the colleague said, shaking his head. Kwame’s chest tightened. He felt the heat rise to his face, certain that his colleague could see what had happened to him, that it was written on his skin like a bruise. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood with his hands on the sink, breathing shallowly, thinking, *Everyone knows. They can tell just by looking at me.* He had come to believe that the assault had permanently marked him, that other people could read the shame in his posture. He felt exposed, constantly. And he felt hollow: there was no future worth planning. He had begun telling himself, *What’s the point? Bad things happen no matter what I do.* He had tried dating once, a woman he met at a conference, but when she invited him to her apartment—a small studio with a door that locked automatically—he had made an excuse and left. He could not imagine being in a confined space with anyone, male or female, without the terror rising.

A year and a half after the assault, Kwame’s clinical work had narrowed. He had stopped accepting new male clients, citing a full caseload. He avoided discussions of sexual violence in supervision, deflecting when the topic came up. His own therapy—he had finally started seeing a counselor three months ago—was the only place he let himself say the word *rape* out loud. He had been referred by a colleague who had noticed his increasing isolation, his refusal to attend team meetings held in a windowless conference room. He had finally come because he had realized, one evening, that he could not remember what it felt like to feel safe. He was afraid that the therapy would not work, that he was too broken to change. But he was more afraid of spending the rest of his life with his back to every wall.
